none.name: No shock
none.note: The world the page assumes, with nothing unusual ahead.

oil_spike.name: Oil price shock
oil_spike.note: Brent doubles for a year and eases back over four, as in 1979-80, 2008 and 2022. Fuel is about a tenth of Iceland's imports, and dearer flights cost some tourism.
sources: Kilian (2009), AER 99(3): oil supply and demand shocks
Hagstofa: fuel's share of goods imports

oil_crash.name: Oil price collapse
oil_crash.note: Brent halves for a year and recovers over four, with metal prices sagging alongside, as in 2015-16 and 2020. Cheaper imports; smelters earn less.
sources: Baffes et al. (2015), World Bank PRN/15/01: the 2014-15 oil price collapse

ai_shock.name: AI jobs shock
ai_shock.note: Automation of cognitive work at the fastest pace the model allows (25% a year cheaper and more capable), from the onset on. The IMF puts about 60% of jobs in advanced economies in reach of AI; the model decides from wages and costs how many are actually replaced.
sources: Cazzaniga et al. (2024), IMF SDN/2024/001: Gen-AI and the future of work
Eloundou et al. (2024), Science 384: GPTs are GPTs
Korinek & Suh (2024), NBER w32255: scenarios for the transition to AGI

amoc.name: Atlantic overturning collapse (AMOC)
amoc.note: The ocean circulation that keeps Iceland mild weakens and collapses over a decade. Winters colder by several degrees, sea ice nearer the coast, fish stocks move: fish earnings fall by up to 30%, tourism by 20%, food and imports cost 10% more, output per worker 2% lower, more people leave and fewer come. Iceland's National Security Council listed a collapse as a national security risk in 2025. The sizes are EST: no economic study of a collapse for Iceland exists yet.
sources: van Westen, Kliphuis & Dijkstra (2024), Science Advances 10: AMOC on tipping course
Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen (2023), Nature Communications 14: collapse likely 2025-2095
Ritchie et al. (2020), Nature Food 1: AMOC collapse and British agriculture
Government of Iceland, National Security Council (2025): AMOC as a security risk

pandemic.name: Pandemic
pandemic.note: Tourism falls by three-quarters for a year and recovers over three, as it did in 2020-22; the state pays the support it paid then (3% and 2% of GDP) and keeps jobs through reduced hours.
sources: Hagstofa: tourism revenue 2019-22
IMF (2021), Iceland Article IV: COVID support

pandemic_shield.name: Pandemic, answered by shielding
pandemic_shield.note: The same pandemic, answered two ways. The status quo answers as Iceland did in 2020. The platform gives no money to firms and keeps the country open: about 30,000 people at high risk are offered 150 þús. a month on top of the payment to live in designated areas — the empty hotels, whose rent the state pays — and some 6,000 young people out of work are paid 650 þús. a month to be on call there. Lives saved are not in the model, which has no deaths from a pandemic; the sizes are estimates for an illustrative alternative response.
sources: Hagstofa: tourism revenue 2019-22
IMF (2021), Iceland Article IV: COVID support
Sweden's and Iceland's 2020 experience of protecting care homes (Directorate of Health)

financial.name: Banking and currency crisis
financial.note: A crisis on the pattern of 2008-10 at about half its depth — Iceland's banks are now about one times GDP, not nine: credit tightens, the bank rate jumps, jobs and output fall, many leave.
sources: Laeven & Valencia (2018), IMF WP/18/206: systemic banking crises database
Hagstofa: 2008-10 output, unemployment and migration

fish_collapse.name: Fish stock collapse
fish_collapse.note: Fish earnings fall by 40% and recover over a decade, as when the herring collapsed in 1967-69 (export earnings fell by nearly half) or the capelin failed in 2019-20.
sources: Jónsson (1994), Economic History of Iceland: the herring collapse
Hafrannsóknastofnun: capelin advice 2019-2020

windfall.name: Resource windfall
windfall.note: Oil, gas or minerals come on stream from the onset and reach a resource rent of 10% of GDP in five years — Norway's scale at its height — taxed at Norway's 78% marginal rate. The export earnings lift the króna, which costs the other export industries (the 'Dutch disease'). Iceland's one search, the Dreki licences on the Jan Mayen ridge (2013-18), was given up, so this is a what-if, not a forecast.
sources: Norwegian Ministry of Finance: the National Budget, petroleum net cash flow
Corden & Neary (1982), Economic Journal 92: booming sector and de-industrialisation
Orkustofnun (2018): relinquishment of the Dreki area licences

events.name: Tourism boom
events.note: Arrivals doubled in three years; a building boom.

events.name: WOW air collapses
events.note: The low-cost airline's fall cut arrivals by a seventh.

events.name: COVID
events.note: Tourism fell by three-quarters; the state paid about 3% of GDP in support.

events.name: Inflation
events.note: Prices rose 8-9% a year; the bank rate went from 0.75% to 9.25%.

events.name: Reykjanes eruptions
events.note: Grindavík evacuated; its housing bought out by the state.
